# The Survey

After Ruth died, Walter discovered that he did not know where anything was.

This surprised him, because he had spent forty-one years as a land surveyor for the county. He had walked every creek bed and fence line within sixty miles. He could tell you, without looking, that the northeast corner of the Hendricks property sat four feet inside the old stone wall, not on it, a fact that had ended a friendship and begun a lawsuit in 1987. He knew where things were. That was his whole profession.

But he did not know where the colander was.

He stood in the kitchen on the ninth day, holding a pot of pasta water that was cooling in his hands, and opened cabinets one by one. Mugs. Plates. A drawer of rubber bands and twist ties and a single birthday candle shaped like the number seven, though no one in the family had turned seven in over thirty years. Baking sheets stacked vertically in a slot he had never noticed. The colander was nowhere. He poured the pasta into a slotted spoon, a few pieces at a time, and ate it standing up, and then he sat at the table and did not move for a long while.

---

The next morning he went out to the garage and found his old equipment. The transit was too much, absurd for a kitchen, but he took the steel tape, the graph paper, the mechanical pencils, the leather field book with its soft, curling corners. He brought them inside and set them on the counter like a man preparing for surgery.

He began at the stove, because a survey needs a point of beginning, and the stove was the one thing in the room that could not be moved.

*Cabinet A, left of range. Lower. Three shelves. Top: cast iron skillet (large), cast iron skillet (small), lid that fits neither.* He paused over that last entry. Why would she keep a lid that fit nothing? He looked at it for some time, turning it in the light. There was a chip in the enamel knob. He wrote it down anyway. A surveyor records what is there, not what makes sense.

It took him four days to do the kitchen.

He found the colander on the second day, on top of the refrigerator, inside a larger mixing bowl, beneath a folded tablecloth. He could not imagine the logic of it. Then he remembered, suddenly and completely, the Thanksgiving three years ago when their daughter had brought her new husband and the kitchen had been too crowded, and Ruth had cleared the counters in a fury of efficiency, putting things anywhere, laughing, saying *I'll sort it out later.* She never had. The colander had lived on top of the refrigerator for three years, and every time she'd needed it she had reached up without thinking, and he had never once seen her do it.

He wrote: *Top of refrigerator. Colander (inside bowl, under cloth). See Thanksgiving.*

---

The field book filled. He moved on to the bathroom, the hall closet, the linen cupboard with its terrible, fragrant order. She had folded fitted sheets into perfect rectangles, which he had always believed to be impossible. He unfolded one to see how it was done and could not get it back. He left it on the bed, a soft white ruin, and felt worse about that than he had felt about some of the larger things.

In her bedside drawer, he found a small notebook of her own.

He almost didn't open it. It felt like trespassing, and he had spent his career on the precise question of where one person's ground ended and another's began. But she was gone, and the boundaries of things had changed, and he opened it.

It was a list. Not a diary, just a list, in her small slanting hand, going back years.

*W. likes the blue mug, not the white, says the white one "tastes wrong."*
*W. won't say he's cold. Watch his shoulders.*
*W. hums when a job went well. Hasn't hummed since the Hendricks thing. (1987)*
*Hummed today! (1988)*
*W. can't find anything. Leave the scissors in the same place ALWAYS.*

He sat on the edge of the bed with the notebook open on his knees.

She had been surveying him. The whole time. Quietly, without instruments, she had walked the lines of him and recorded what was there, whether or not it made sense. The lid that fit nothing. The mug that tasted wrong. For forty-four years she had kept a map of the territory of Walter, and she had used it to arrange the world so that he could move through it without noticing the arrangement at all.

He had thought he was a man who knew where things were. He had simply been a man who was always, lovingly, put in the right place.

---

He did not finish the survey of the house. There seemed no point. Some of it, he understood now, could not be mapped from the outside. It could only be known the way she had known it, by attention paid over time, by watching someone's shoulders.

But he kept the field book on the kitchen counter, and some evenings he added to it. Not the location of objects anymore. Other things.

*Daughter calls Sundays. Sounds tired. Ask about work.*
*Neighbor's boy mows lawn, won't take money. Find out what he likes.*
*Cardinal at the feeder, 7:15, most mornings. Ruth would have named it.*

He named it Hendricks, which would have made her laugh.

And he put the colander back on top of the refrigerator, inside the bowl, beneath the cloth, because that was where it went.

Actually, I'll go with fiction instead—"The Cartographer of Small Things," about a retired surveyor mapping his kitchen after his wife's death because she was the one who always knew where everything was. That feels right; I'll write around 1000 words on it.
